source.title: Discovering Cross-Language Reasoning Invariance in LLMs with Geometry-Invariant Sparse Autoencoders

page_placements.theme: Conditional cross-model feature sharing and alignment

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present; no material garbling or cutoff is evident.
record.tranche_reason: Tests cross-language SAE feature sharing in five LLMs on multilingual math reasoning, an LLM setting distinct from the toy networks in the original superposition work. It does not test toy-model superposition itself.
record.gate_note: The study trains baseline and contrastive SAEs, measures cross-language feature sharing, and causally patches shared feature values. The causal interchangeability results do not measure any listed version directly, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. Per-layer values are reported in Appendix B; the rows below retain the model-level ranges and summaries stated in the main text, rather than treating layer observations as a single average.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAEs (baseline and its own contrastive GI-SAE) as tools to measure cross-language feature sharing and causal interchangeability in five LLMs. It never asks whether features are superposed, whether neurons are polysemantic, whether a dictionary recovers more sparse features than dimensions, or whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical. Cross-language shared fraction is a different construct: which dictionary indices co-activate for the same problem across languages. The Appendix I audit is a sanity check that the tool's features are meaningful, not a test of V4. None of V1–V6 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that cross-language feature sharing varies strongly by model (progressive in Qwen, saturated in Gemma, mixed in Llama and Phi). GI-SAE improves CKA almost everywhere but improves KL/feature only where baseline sharing is moderate (83% vs 6% saturated). Geometric similarity should not be used as a proxy for functional interchangeability.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains reconstruction-only and contrastive top-K SAEs on LLM residual-stream activations and uses cross-language feature patching. It does not use the original toy-network superposition setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model and layer; GI-SAE benefit differs by baseline sharing profile. The normalized-space patching check preserves Qwen/convergent results but flips some individual low- or mixed-profile layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Baseline-SAE cross-language shared fraction differs sharply by model: Gemma 87–96%, Qwen 11–62% rising with depth, Phi 1–17%, Llama 4–6%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How many SAE features LLMs share across languages for the same reasoning problem depends strongly on model family and depth.

fits_no_version.finding: GI-SAE raises CKA at nearly every layer, but lowers KL/feature only in the convergent profile (83% win rate). The win rate is 6% in the saturated profile.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometric similarity of SAE codes across languages does not imply that shared feature values are functionally interchangeable.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
record.problems: Results are conditional on problems solved correctly with extractable reasoning in all six languages; valid counts are only 60 for Llama and 63 for Phi, versus 151–202 for Qwen. The paper notes that layer observations within models are correlated, its taxonomy is based on only one checkpoint for each non-Qwen family, and some low/mixed-profile results are patching-convention-sensitive. GI-SAE training also has higher validation reconstruction loss and reduced alive-feature fractions in some layers.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix B reports 78 per-layer observations, including layer-specific shared fractions, KL/feature, and AFR. These detailed per-layer entries are not reproduced individually; the model-level ranges, win summaries, and reported qualitative audits are retained in r1–r17.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity sweep or feature geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity/importance analysis.
No analysis of the causes of polysemantic neurons.
No measure of features spread across neurons. No test that the SAE recovers sparse features beyond dimensions or against a ground truth; SAEs are used as given.
No comparison of feature identity across seeds, sizes or objectives; no completeness or canonicality test.
No comparison of one-dimensional with multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: GI-SAE training costs: GI-SAE validation reconstruction loss is 1.3–4.2× baseline, and its alive features drop to 84–88% in some layers. This matters only if a version on SAE objectives (V5) is later added.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T3 to uses_without_test/T4. The study takes SAE features as its unit of analysis and never evaluates superposition or SAE validity in a way any version names. The reader's V4 'supports' label is removed: nonzero cross-language sharing and a handful of interpretable boundary features do not bear on whether models contain dictionary-recoverable sparse features in superposition. Row r6 cites a Qwen3-1.7B audit that does not exist in Table 15.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, more sparse features than dimensions, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether neuron polysemanticity results from competition for limited capacity or from feature importance.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The study examines SAE features, not whether features are spread across many neurons. It does not assess SAE recoverability against a ground-truth feature set.
Completeness, stability across SAE training runs or dictionaries, and canonicality of SAE features are not tested.
The study intervenes on individual SAE feature values but does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

relation.reason: The study uses sparse dictionary representations without testing superposition, capacity-driven polysemanticity, dictionary completeness or canonicality, or feature dimensionality.

tranche.reason: SAEs serve as tools for measuring cross-language sharing and evaluating GI-SAE functional interchangeability; these results do not test a listed superposition claim version.

source_check.notes: Sharing ranges match Table 3's reported summaries and describe co-activation, not superposition; GI-SAE comparisons evaluate the study's own method. Results are conditional on problems solved correctly with extractable reasoning in all six languages.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SAE analyses across the five tested models; representative cross-language feature audits
reader_labels.reason: The study reports nonzero cross-language SAE feature sharing across models and audits shared features with multilingual discourse, answer-boundary, and reasoning-step examples (r1–r10). This supports the SAE-recoverable-feature branch of V4, not its neuron-spreading branch.
